name: Waitangi Treaty Grounds
description:
The place where Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, was first signed in 1840, on a grassy headland just north of Paihia. Admission covers a 50 minute guided tour, a 30 minute Māori cultural performance, the Treaty House, the carved meeting house Te Whare Rūnanga, the world's largest ceremonial waka and two museums: Te Kōngahu Museum of Waitangi, and Te Rau Aroha, which tells the story of Māori who served in war.

New prices started on 1 October 2026. New Zealand residents pay $39 for adults and $19.50 for youth aged 13 to 17 (bring ID), while international visitors pay $78 and $39. Children 12 and under are free with a paying adult, and your ticket is valid for two days in a row. From 26 December to 28 February the performance runs six times a day, at 11am, 12pm, 1pm, 2.30pm, 3.30pm and 4.30pm. The Whare Waka café is closed, but a coffee cart runs daily from 10am to 3pm.
Local tip: Join the 10am tour and then the 11am performance, which run all year, and save the museums for the second day of your ticket. Allow at least three hours on your first visit.
hoursNote: Daily 9am to 5pm (1 Mar to 24 Dec), 9am to 6pm (26 Dec to 28 Feb); closed Christmas Day; buildings closed on Waitangi Day (6 Feb) for the free festival; performances 11am, 1pm and 3pm outside summer

name: Haruru Falls
description:
A wide, horseshoe shaped waterfall about 5m high on the Waitangi River, roughly 3km inland from Waitangi off Puketona Road. There's a car park with a picnic area, and the lookout over the falls is about two minutes' walk away.

You can also walk here from Waitangi. The track starts at the northern end of the Waitangi Treaty Grounds land, opposite the visitor centre, and runs through kānuka forest and along a boardwalk through the mangroves beside the river. It's easy, about 5 to 6km one way, and takes about 2 hours each way.
Local tip: The mangrove boardwalk gets slippery when wet, so wear shoes with good grip, and arrange a lift back from the falls if you'd rather not walk both ways.
hoursNote: Open any time; free parking and toilets at the falls; Waitangi to Haruru Falls track about 5km one way

name: Hole in the Rock Dolphin Cruise
description:
The classic Bay of Islands boat trip, run by Fullers from Paihia with a pick up at Russell. The boat weaves through the islands and along the Cape Brett peninsula, past the lighthouse, to Motukōkako, the Hole in the Rock, and when the sea allows, the skipper takes it right through the arch. The crew watch for dolphins and whales all the way, but swimming with dolphins isn't allowed in the bay.

The cruise takes 4.5 hours, including about 1.5 hours ashore at Otehei Bay on Urupukapuka Island. Adults are $180, children 5 to 15 are $90, under 5s are free, and a family pass for two adults and two children is $450. On May to September departures, a marine mammal guarantee gives you a free return trip if you see no dolphins or whales.
Local tip: On the morning cruise you can stay on Urupukapuka and come back on a later boat at no extra cost. Arrange it with Fullers on 0800 653 339.
hoursNote: Daily; Sep to May departs Paihia 8.30am and 2pm (Russell 10 minutes later); Jun to Aug 10am only; going through the arch depends on sea conditions

name: Urupukapuka Island
description:
At 208ha, the largest island in the Bay of Islands, and pest free, so you hear tūī and can spot birds such as tīeke (saddleback) and toutouwai (North Island robin), returned here by Project Island Song. The Urupukapuka Island Walk circles the island past old Māori archaeological sites, sheltered bays, bush and clifftop views. DOC grades it easy, and the full loop takes about five hours, but you can walk any part of it from Otehei Bay, where the ferry lands.

The Otehei Bay ferry from Explore takes 40 minutes each way and costs $80 return for adults, $45 for children 5 to 15 and $205 for a family. From September it leaves Paihia at 8.30am, 10am, 11.30am, 2pm and 5pm, calling at Russell 10 minutes later, and heads back from Otehei Bay at 10.45am, 12.15pm, 1.45pm, 4.15pm and 5.45pm. Otehei Bay has a licensed café and bar, and kayak, snorkel and paddleboard hire in summer.
Local tip: Check your bags and gear for pests before you board, and take your rubbish home. The Whangapau Point pā track is closed after a slip.
hoursNote: Ferry daily from Paihia and Russell, timetable varies with demand; no dogs on the island; DOC conservation centre at Otehei Bay open 26 Dec to 6 Feb

name: Ōpua to Ōkiato Car Ferry
description:
The quickest way to drive to Russell. The vehicle ferry crosses the narrow channel between Ōpua, about seven minutes' drive south of Paihia, and Ōkiato, about ten minutes' drive from Russell. The crossing takes ten minutes, and you just join the queue and pay on board by EFTPOS or card.

A car or campervan under 6m is $19.80 one way, and everyone inside travels free. A motorbike is $9.70, a 6 to 8m campervan $33.80, and foot passengers pay $2.70 for adults and $1.60 for children 5 to 14. If you're on foot, the Paihia to Russell passenger ferry is $19.40 return for adults and takes 15 minutes.
Local tip: Make a loop of it. Walk the coastal track from Paihia to Ōpua, cross on the car ferry, then take the passenger ferry from Russell back to Paihia.
hoursNote: Daily; first sailing 6.10am from Ōpua (6am from Ōkiato), last 10pm from Ōpua (9.50pm from Ōkiato); about every 10 minutes by day, every 20 minutes early and late

name: Pompallier Mission and Printery
description:
A French style rammed earth building on the Russell waterfront that was the hub of the Catholic mission in New Zealand. The brothers here tanned leather, printed and bound books in te reo Māori, and Heritage New Zealand guides walk you through each step using the original tools and press.

Tours are small, and depending on the season you may get to pull your own print on the old French press. In summer, guided tours run at 10.30am, 11.30am, 1.30pm, 2.30pm and 3.30pm (there's no 3.30pm tour in winter). Adults pay $20, under 18s go free, and a garden-only visit is $10.
Local tip: Christ Church, New Zealand's oldest surviving church, is a two minute walk away, so see both on the same visit.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 4.30pm (Nov to Apr), 10am to 3.30pm (May to Oct); closed Christmas Day; entry from $20

name: Christ Church, Russell
description:
New Zealand's oldest surviving church, built in 1835 in what was then Kororāreka. It's a small, simple wooden church in a leafy graveyard, and services were held here in both Māori and English from the start. Look for the musket ball holes in the walls left by the fighting of 1845.

The church is open to visitors on most days, and entry is by donation, with an EFTPOS terminal inside if you have no cash. The graveyard holds sailors from HMS Hazard killed in the 1845 battle, and the Ngāpuhi chief Tāmati Wāka Nene is buried here too. The Sunday service is at 10.30am.
Local tip: It's a working church, so keep your visit quiet if a service, funeral or wedding is on.
hoursNote: Usually open daily about 9am to 5pm (Sundays from 10.30am); entry by donation

name: Flagstaff Hill (Maiki)
description:
The hill above Russell where the British flagstaff was cut down four times in 1844 and 1845, first by Te Haratua and then by Hōne Heke and his men. The last felling, on 11 March 1845, came with the attack on Kororāreka, the opening of the Northern War. Today it's a DOC historic reserve with a 360 degree view over Russell, Paihia and the islands.

The DOC track up from town is easy and takes about 30 minutes, starting at the corner of Wellington and Kent streets by the boat ramp on the Strand. A beach route via Watering Bay is passable at low tide only. You can also drive to a car park at the base of the summit path, but Wellington Street is very narrow. Dogs aren't allowed, even on a lead, on the private land the track crosses.
Local tip: Walk up in the late afternoon for the best light over the bay, and bring water on a hot day.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; walk about 30 minutes each way from Russell, or drive to the car park near the top

name: Long Beach (Oneroa Bay), Russell
description:
Russell's swimming beach, a curved bay of soft sand on the other side of the hill from the town. Swimming is easy at all tides, so it suits families, but the beach isn't patrolled.

It's about 1.5km from the township, around 20 minutes on foot over the hill or five minutes by car, and there's a free car park by the beach that fills on busy summer days. There are wheelchair accessible toilets and a surfboard shaped outdoor shower, but no cafés, so bring your own food and drink.
Local tip: Skip swimming for two to three days after heavy rain, when water quality drops.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; toilets and outdoor shower; limited parking

name: Russell Fish Co
description:
A small takeaway at 2 Cass Street, just off the Russell waterfront, and a favourite with reviewers for its beer battered fish and chips. The salt and pepper squid also gets plenty of praise.

It's takeaway only, so carry your parcel across to the Strand and eat on the seawall looking out over the boats. Some reviewers find it pricey, but most say the quality is worth it. It's open Wednesday to Sunday from 11am to 7.30pm.
Local tip: It's closed on Mondays and Tuesdays, and keep a close eye on your chips, as the gulls on the waterfront are bold.
hoursNote: Wed to Sun 11am to 7.30pm; closed Mon and Tue; takeaway

name: Paihia to Ōpua Coastal Walkway
description:
A coastal walk between Paihia and the port at Ōpua, with sea views most of the way and a section of Te Araroa, the trail that runs the length of the country. It mixes beach, rocky shore, boardwalks over the water and through the mangroves, and short climbs through shady bush, and you can watch the ferries crossing to Russell as you go.

It's about 5km one way and takes 1.5 to 2 hours in each direction. Slips and storm damage have closed sections of the track for repairs in recent years, including a stretch between Walls Bay and Lemons Bay after Cyclone Gabrielle.
Local tip: Check Far North District Council's website for track closures before you set out, then finish with lunch in Paihia or carry on over to Russell on the car ferry.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; about 7km one way; some sections tidal; short section near Ōpua closed by rockfalls, detour by road

name: Stone Store and Kemp House, Kerikeri
description:
Kerikeri Mission Station, set up in 1819 beside the Kerikeri River basin, below Kororipo Pā. Kemp House, finished in 1822, is New Zealand's oldest surviving building, and the Stone Store next to it is the country's oldest stone building. Both are cared for by Heritage New Zealand.

The ground floor of the Stone Store is a shop of gifts and old fashioned goods that's free to enter. A $20 adult ticket covers a guided tour of Kemp House (the only way to see inside) and the self-guided museum upstairs in the Stone Store, and under 18s go free with an adult. It's open daily from 10am to 5pm from November to April, and 10am to 4pm from May to October.
Local tip: The Kerikeri River Track to Rainbow Falls starts here, so pair your visit with the walk.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 5pm (Nov to Apr), 10am to 4pm (May to Oct); Kemp House visits from $20; shop and grounds free

name: Rainbow Falls and Kerikeri River Track
description:
A curtain of water dropping into a deep pool in the bush on the edge of Kerikeri. From the car park at the end of Rainbow Falls Road, an easy 400m path (about 10 minutes, fine for wheelchairs and buggies) leads to three viewing points: two look over the falls and the third sits by a historic weir. There are toilets and picnic areas at the car park.

For a longer walk, the DOC Kerikeri River Track follows the river from Kerikeri Basin, by the Stone Store, to Rainbow Falls. It's 3.5km one way, graded easy, and takes about 1.5 hours each way, passing Wharepoke Falls, the Fairy Pools, young kauri and the remains of a hydro power station that ran from 1930 to 1967. Dogs aren't allowed.
Local tip: The river track has steep drops and narrow sections, so keep children close, and DOC warns against swimming near the falls and weirs.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; no dogs; toilets at the Rainbow Falls Road car park; track about 3.5km one way from Kerikeri Basin

name: Bay of Islands Farmers' Market, Kerikeri
description:
A Sunday morning growers' market in the Post Office car park at 10 Hobson Avenue in central Kerikeri, running from 8.30am to 12pm. Stalls sell local fruit and vegetables straight from the grower, plus cheese, preserves, free range eggs, plants, fresh baking and freshly squeezed orange juice, and there's locally roasted coffee.

It's small and friendly rather than big, and a good way to stock up on fresh local produce. In Paihia, the same group runs a market on the Village Green on Thursdays from October to April, 10am to 1.30pm.
Local tip: Go early for the best produce. If you miss it, Kerikeri Bakehouse at 334 Kerikeri Road is open daily from 7am to 3pm.
hoursNote: Sundays 8.30am to 12pm, Post Office car park, 10 Hobson Ave, Kerikeri; Paihia market Thursdays Oct to Apr 10am to 1.30pm

name: Hundertwasser Toilets, Kawakawa
description:
Probably the most photographed public toilets in the country, on the main street of Kawakawa, about 20 minutes' drive from Paihia. The Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser, who lived near Kawakawa from 1975 until his death in 2000, designed them, and they were finished in 1999. Expect irregular ceramic tiles, coloured glass bottles set into the walls and hardly a straight line anywhere.

They're free, working public toilets. Behind them is Te Hononga, opened in October 2020 in the same spirit, with the town library (open weekdays 8am to 4.30pm and Saturdays 9am to 1pm), WiFi, and a shower and toilet block open 24 hours.
Local tip: Time your stop for 11am or 2.30pm on a day the vintage train runs, when it sets off down the middle of the main street right past the toilets.
hoursNote: Open daily about 7am to 10pm; free

name: Bay of Islands Vintage Railway
description:
A heritage train from Kawakawa that starts by rolling slowly down the middle of the town's main street, then heads out past Taumarere to the Whangae Tunnel platform. The return trip takes about two hours, in a mix of covered and open carriages, and the Railway Station Café is open daily.

Fares from 1 October 2026 are $65 for adults, $55 for seniors, $25 for children 3 to 17 and $170 for a family of two adults and two children, and under 3s ride free. Bikes can come along, with a one way cycle connection for $25 adult or $15 child, so you can ride one way and take the train the other. You can also hire a bike at the station for $15 an hour, $65 a day, or $85 including the train. Tickets are fully refundable or transferable.
Local tip: Book ahead, as services may not run if nobody has booked, and arrive 15 minutes before departure.
hoursNote: 25 Sep to 18 Dec: Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat and Sun, departs Kawakawa 11am and 2.30pm; summer timetable daily with two trains a day from 19 Dec

name: Matauri Bay
description:
A long beach of white sand and clear water north of Kerikeri, looking out to the Cavalli Islands. It's good for swimming and snorkelling, and there are public toilets and free parking. The northern end is the calmer side for families, while the southern end picks up surf in a north east or east swell.

A short, steep track through Matauri Bay Holiday Park climbs to the Rainbow Warrior memorial by Chris Booth on the headland, dedicated in 1990. The Greenpeace ship, bombed in Auckland in 1985, was scuttled off the Cavalli Islands in 1987 at a depth of about 25m and is now a dive site.
Local tip: There are no shops or cafés apart from the holiday park's general store, so bring food, water and shade.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; toilets and parking; memorial track starts in the holiday park; mobile coverage is poor at the beach

name: St Paul's Rock (Ohakiri), Whangaroa
description:
A rocky dome above the small fishing village of Whangaroa, known to DOC as Ohakiri Pā, with sweeping views over the twisting arms of Whangaroa Harbour, the bush clad hills and out to sea. The track starts from the car park at the end of Old Hospital Road.

The walk up takes about 30 minutes one way. DOC grades it easy but says you need moderate fitness, as the path is steep and slippery in places, with steps over a fence. The last 30m is a scramble up rock using fixed chains, so it's not for everyone, and the summit has vertical drops with no barriers.
Local tip: Wear shoes with good grip, skip the chains after heavy rain, and keep children close at the top.
hoursNote: Open any time; free; steep track with chains on the final rock; limited parking at the top of Old Hospital Road

name: Kawakawa Freedom Camping (Te Hononga car park)
description:
A free overnight spot in the council car park behind the Hundertwasser toilets and Te Hononga in Kawakawa. Overnight camping isn't allowed on Far North District Council parks, reserves and beaches, so this is a handy option near Paihia.

Te Hononga has a shower and toilet block open 24 hours for campers, and campers report free cold showers and hot showers at $4 for six minutes. The main street takeaways are a minute's walk away, and there's a dump station and water on Waiomio Road nearby. Expect to need a certified self-contained vehicle with a green warrant, as blue warrants stopped being valid on 7 June 2026.
Local tip: Read the signs at the car park for the current rules, and arrive by late afternoon in summer.
hoursNote: Free; vehicles only, no tents; about 14 bays; toilets, cold shower free, hot shower $4; check on-site signs for self-containment rules

name: Urupukapuka Bay Campsite (DOC)
description:
A DOC campsite on a sheltered beach on pest free Urupukapuka Island, reached by ferry or water taxi to Otehei Bay and then a 15 minute uphill walk. There are 60 tent sites in four zones and a composting toilet, and the Otehei Bay café is over the hill. Ferries run daily in peak summer, and water taxis all year.

It costs $18 a night for adults and $9 for children 5 to 17, rising to $20 and $10 from 26 December to 8 February, and under 5s are free. You must book online before you arrive, as no spaces are kept for walk ins. No fires, dogs, drones or generators are allowed, so bring a gas cooker. A paid rubbish barge runs from Boxing Day to Waitangi weekend, and at other times you take all your rubbish back to the mainland.
Local tip: Book well ahead for December to February, and check your gear for pests before you leave the mainland.
hoursNote: Booking required; tents only; adults $18, children $9 (summer peak $20 and $10); no dogs or fires; camp host 26 Dec to Waitangi weekend

name: Puriri Bay Campsite (DOC), Whangaruru
description:
A quiet DOC campsite at the end of the road on Whangaruru North Head, on the coast south east of Russell. Sites run along a calm beach, and walking tracks into the scenic reserve start from the camp.

It costs $20 a night for adults and $10 for children 5 to 17, and under 5s are free. Book online before you arrive, check in from 2pm and check out by 11am. Camp hosts are on site from Labour Weekend to the end of April. Outside that time, one toilet block stays open, the grass is closed and only the hard ground parking is used. There's no rubbish collection (the nearest drop offs are at Oakura and Russell), and the nearest medical centre is in Russell. The Picnic Bay to Puriri Bay track is closed by a slip, so walk the road instead.
Local tip: There are no shops nearby, so stock up in Russell or Paihia first, and watch for wasps on the tracks.
hoursNote: Booking required; adults $20, children $10; hosts Labour Weekend to end of April; no rubbish collection; Picnic Bay to Puriri Bay track closed, walk the road instead

name: Bay of Islands Lodge, Paihia
description:
A Kiwi owned, solar powered budget lodge at 11 MacMurray Road in central Paihia, about 250m from the beach, cafés and wharf. It has private rooms only, no dorms, and every room has its own ensuite and free WiFi, with rooms for solos, couples, groups and families.

Guests share a kitchen, a lounge and a covered courtyard with picnic tables and a barbecue. Rooms are listed from about $79 to $160 a night. Recent reviews praise the friendly owner and the cleanliness, though some find the rooms and bathrooms small.
Local tip: It's an easy walk to the ferry and tour boats, so you can leave the car parked for your whole stay.
hoursNote: Private ensuite rooms only, no dorms; from about $79 a night; shared kitchen and BBQ
